items.title: Origins of Bhakti & the Saguna–Nirguna Divide
items.body:
## Roots of the Movement

- The **Bhakti movement** emphasised **devotion (bhakti)** and a **personal bond with God**, rejecting caste hierarchy and empty ritual.
- It first flowered in **South India (7th–12th centuries CE)** through the **Nayanars** (Shaiva) and **Alvars** (Vaishnava), as a **revival of theistic Hinduism** resisting Jainism and Buddhism, and later spread north.
- Drivers: oppression under the varna system, dissatisfaction of artisans/lower castes, the influence of **Islamic monotheism and Sufi liberalism**, and the difficulty of Shankara's abstract Advaita for common people.

## Two Streams

| Aspect | Saguna Bhakti | Nirguna Bhakti |
|---|---|---|
| God | With form & attributes (Rama, Krishna) | Formless, attribute-less Brahman |
| Saints | Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Vallabhacharya | Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ravidas |
| Worship | Idol worship, festivals, bhajans/kirtans | Meditation, chanting (nam/zikr), rejects idolatry |

- Both streams stressed **equality, vernacular expression and a direct path to God**.
keyPoints: Bhakti stresses personal devotion and equality; first flourished in South India (7th–12th c.) via Nayanars and Alvars.
It arose as a revival of Hinduism resisting Jainism and Buddhism and rigid caste ritualism.
Saguna Bhakti = devotion to a God with form (Rama/Krishna) — Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Vallabhacharya.
Nirguna Bhakti = devotion to a formless God — Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ravidas.
Sufi monotheism and liberalism influenced the rise of the Bhakti movement.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Bhakti Movement in North & South India

items.title: South Indian Bhakti: Alvars, Nayanars & the Acharyas
items.body:
## Alvars & Nayanars

| | Nayanars | Alvars |
|---|---|---|
| Devotion | Shiva | Vishnu |
| Number | 63 saints | 12 saints (incl. Andal) |
| Hymns | **Tevaram** | **Nalayira Divya Prabandham** (4000 Tamil verses) |
| Women saint | Karaikkal Ammaiyar | Andal |

- Both used **Tamil**, criticised Brahmanical ritual monopoly, and popularised **pilgrimage & sacred geography**. Alvar hymns became the base of **Srivaishnavism**.

## The Three Acharyas (Vedanta schools)

| Philosopher | School | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Adi Shankaracharya** (8th c.) | Advaita (Non-Dualism) | Atman = Brahman; world is Maya. Founded 4 mathas — Badrinath (N), Puri (E), Dwarka (W), Sringeri (S) |
| **Ramanujacharya** (1017–1137) | Vishishtadvaita (Qualified Monism) | Souls distinct but connected to Brahman; founded Srivaishnava sect; opposed mayavada |
| **Madhvacharya** (1238–1317) | Dvaita (Dualism) | Soul & Brahman eternally distinct; world is real |

## Virashaivism / Lingayatism

- **Basavanna** (12th c.) founded **Lingayatism** in Karnataka — worship of the **Ishtalinga**, rejection of caste, temples and idols; **Vachana** poetry (Kannada) and the **Anubhava Mantapa**. **Akka Mahadevi** and **Allama Prabhu** were key mystics.
keyPoints: Alvars = 12 Vaishnava saints (Nalayira Divya Prabandham, 4000 verses); Nayanars = 63 Shaiva saints (Tevaram).
Andal (Alvar) and Karaikkal Ammaiyar (Nayanar) were prominent women saints.
Shankaracharya = Advaita and founded four mathas: Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, Sringeri.
Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita (Srivaishnava); Madhva = Dvaita (soul & Brahman eternally distinct).
Basavanna founded Lingayatism (Ishtalinga worship, Vachana poetry, Anubhava Mantapa) in 12th-c. Karnataka.
items.mnemonic: Acharya order by 'distance from oneness': Shankara (one) → Ramanuja (qualified) → Madhva (two/dual).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Bhakti Movement in South India

items.title: Northern & Maharashtra Bhakti Saints
items.body:
## North Indian Saints

| Saint | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Ramananda** (c.1486–1533) | Ram Bhakti in vernacular; accepted disciples of all castes (Kabir, Ravidas) — the bridge to northern Bhakti |
| **Kabir** (15th c.) | Nirguna; attacked idolatry, caste, ritual; verses in *Bijak*, *Kabir Granthavali*, *Adi Granth*; cryptic *Ulatbansi* |
| **Tulsidas** (1511–1623) | Saguna Rama Bhakti; *Ramcharitmanas* (Awadhi); Ramleela, Sankatmochan temple |
| **Surdas** (1483–1563) | Krishna devotee; *Sursagar*; disciple of Vallabhacharya |
| **Mirabai** | Rajput princess; Krishna bhajans defying social norms |
| **Vallabhacharya** (1479–1531) | Founded *Pushtimarga* (Way of Grace); Shuddha-Dvaita |

## Maharashtra (Varkari) Tradition — 13th–17th c.

- Centred on **Vithoba (Vitthal) of Pandharpur**; composed **Abhangas** in simple Marathi.
- **Dnyaneshwar (1275–1296):** *Dnyaneshwari* (Marathi commentary on the Gita), *Amrutanubhav*; Nath tradition.
- **Namdev:** hymns in the **Guru Granth Sahib**; stressed family life.
- **Eknath:** *Eknathi Bhagavata*; compassion and tolerance.
- **Tukaram (17th c.):** worshipper of Vithoba; Abhangas of humanism and social reform.
- **Chokhamela** (Mahar caste) & **Soyarabai** voiced protest against untouchability. **Ramdas** (Dasbodh) guided Shivaji.
keyPoints: Ramananda carried Bhakti to North India and took disciples across castes, including Kabir and Ravidas.
Kabir (Nirguna) criticised caste/ritual; works in Bijak, Kabir Granthavali and the Adi Granth.
Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi); Surdas wrote Sursagar; Vallabhacharya founded the Pushtimarga sect.
Maharashtra Varkari saints worship Vithoba at Pandharpur and compose Abhangas.
Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari; Namdev's hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib; Tukaram composed reformist Abhangas.
items.mnemonic: Maharashtra Varkari 'DNET': Dnyaneshwar → Namdev → Eknath → Tukaram.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Bhakti in North India & Saints of Maharashtra

items.title: Sufism: Concepts, Silsilahs & Impact
items.body:
## Core Ideas

- **Sufism** = mystical Islam; a spiritual journey under a **pir/murshid** to achieve communion with God, stressing love and purity of heart.
- The disciple (**murid**) passes through **maqamat** (stages). The **khanqah** (hospice) was the centre of activity and a hub of learning; after a saint's death his **dargah** (shrine) became a pilgrimage site, celebrated on the **urs**.
- By the 12th century Sufism organised into **silsilahs** (orders). Ibn-i-Arabi's **Wahdat-ul-Wajud** (Unity of Being) was influential.

## Major Silsilahs

| Order | Founder in India | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Chishti** | Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, after 1192) | Love, tolerance, simplicity; **avoided politics**; embraced sama; Nizamuddin Auliya, Amir Khusrau |
| **Suhrawardi** | Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan) | **Close ties with the state**; accepted grants/posts; rejected sama |
| **Naqshbandi** | (Bahauddin Naqshbandi) | Strict Islamic law; opposed sama & shrine pilgrimage; **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** criticised Akbar |
| **Qadiri** | Sheikh Abdul Qadir | Wahdat al-Wujud; **Miyan Mir** enrolled Dara Shikoh & Jahanara |

## Cultural Impact

- Promoted **equality, brotherhood and service to the poor** (Nizamuddin Auliya).
- Boosted **regional literature**: **Baba Farid** (Punjabi, verses in the Adi Granth), **Amir Khusrau** (Hindawi, Persian metres, style *sabaq-i-hindi*, pioneer of qawwali).
keyPoints: Sufism is mystical Islam: a murid seeks God under a pir/murshid, passing through maqamat (stages).
Key terms: khanqah (hospice), silsilah (order), sama (music), dargah (shrine), urs (death anniversary), fanaa (self-annihilation).
Chishti (Muinuddin Chishti, Ajmer) avoided politics and embraced sama; Nizamuddin Auliya and Amir Khusrau belonged to it.
Suhrawardi kept state ties; Naqshbandi (Sirhindi) was orthodox and anti-sama; Qadiri's Miyan Mir taught Dara Shikoh.
Sufis enriched vernacular literature — Baba Farid (Punjabi) and Amir Khusrau (Hindawi/qawwali, sabaq-i-hindi).
items.mnemonic: Silsilah stance on sama: Chishti YES, Suhrawardi/Naqshbandi NO.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Sufism

items.title: Telugu Bhakti Poet-Saints (AP focus)
items.body:
## Devotional Poets of the Telugu Country

| Poet-saint | Period | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Annamacharya (Annamayya)** | 1408–1503 | Earliest known composer of **Telugu sankirtanas** (~32,000) on **Lord Venkateswara of Tirumala–Tirupati**; revered as *Pada Kavita Pitamaha*; works engraved on copper plates |
| **Bammera Potana** | c. 1450–1510 | Rendered the Bhagavata Purana into Telugu as **Andhra Mahabhagavatamu**; a Rama devotee who dedicated his work to God, not a king |
| **Vemana (Yogi Vemana)** | c. 15th–17th c. | Aphoristic **Vemana Satakam** (ataveladi metre); attacked caste, ritual and hypocrisy; refrain *'Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema'* |
| **Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna)** | 17th c. | Rama **keertanas**; rebuilt the **Bhadrachalam temple**; imprisoned by the **Golconda Sultan (Abul Hasan Tanisha)** |
| **Tyagaraja** | 1767–1847 | One of the **Trinity of Carnatic music**; Telugu **kritis** in devotion to Rama (Pancharatna kritis) |

- These saint-poets carried Bhakti devotion into **Telugu vernacular literature and Carnatic music**, and are heavily AP-examinable.
keyPoints: Annamacharya (1408–1503): earliest Telugu sankirtana composer, devotee of Venkateswara (Tirupati), 'Pada Kavita Pitamaha'.
Bammera Potana rendered the Bhagavata into Telugu as the Andhra Mahabhagavatamu.
Vemana wrote the aphoristic Vemana Satakam critiquing caste and ritual (refrain 'Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema').
Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna) built the Bhadrachalam temple and was jailed by the Golconda ruler Tanisha.
Tyagaraja (1767–1847) is one of the Carnatic Trinity; his Telugu kritis are largely devoted to Rama.
items.source: APPSC standard references — Telugu Bhakti poets (Annamacharya, Potana, Vemana, Ramadasu, Tyagaraja)
